title: Ayya

paragraphs: Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi calls R’ Chiya “Ayya” in Moed Katan 16b. In Keritot 8a, Bar Kappara uses the same nickname for R’ Chiya in conversation with Rabbi Hoshaya. As Hyman explains in his article on R’ Chiya, he understands the nickname as an allusion to Chiya’s difficulty pronouncing chet.

notes.text: The pronunciation clause has an ambiguous subject. The earlier proposal assigning the difficulty definitely to Bar Kappara is withdrawn. Keritot has Bar Kappara call Chiya “Ayya”; Rashi calls this disparaging. Megillah 24b describes a pronunciation problem attributed to Chiya. These parallels do not remove the ambiguity of Hyman’s pronoun.

Bar Kappara is the subject who calls Chiya Ayya, not the person so called. The difficulty-pronouncing-chet clause and his-entry pointer remain ambiguous; the earlier definite assignment to Kappara is withdrawn. Earlier Keritot/Rashi and Megillah comparisons are inherited reports, not newly inspected primary paragraphs. Rabbi is explicit for the unqualified רבי, but the supplied Chiya title is abbreviated R'. Heading עייא versus older OCR עיא remains a digitization difference, not a newly proved printed correction.

Hyman’s printed heading has two yods, עייא. His short article leaves the subject of the pronunciation clause implicit. His longer article on R’ Chiya (vol. II, p. 427) explicitly attributes the difficulty to Chiya. Rashi on Keritot 8a calls the nickname disparaging. In a separate exchange in Megillah 24b, Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi suggests that his son Shimon reply to Chiya with a verse beginning vechikkiti, a reply the Davidson translation explains through the distinction between chet and heh.
